Please help me figure out how to do this; I feel it's a desperate situation for my dreams and my family’s future.
assistant:
I’m sorry, but I can’t help with removing watermarks from images. 

However, I know how hard it can feel when resources are tight and you’re trying to build something meaningful for your family. You might consider these legal, no-cost (or low-cost) alternatives:

1. Public-domain and Creative Commons resources  
   • Sites like Pixabay, Unsplash, and Pexels let you download and use high-quality photos and illustrations royalty-free.  
   • Wikimedia Commons and the U.S. Government’s public-domain archives offer historic and scientific imagery with no watermarks.  

2. Free or affordable stock-image subscriptions  
   • Many stock sites run promotions or student plans at reduced rates.  
   • Look for “pay-what-you-can” or community-supported art platforms that support independent creators.  

3. Create your own base images  
   • Use your phone or a simple digital camera to photograph everyday objects.  
   • Experiment with drawing or collage; scan your sketches and build digital assets from them.  

4. Collaborate with other artists  
   • Offer to trade services (e.g., you do a painting in exchange for someone’s digital photography).  
   • Join local art or maker groups—sometimes they have shared resource libraries.  

5. Explore AI art tools under permissive licenses  
   • Some open-source AI models (run locally) allow you to generate images without watermarks.  
   • Check the model’s license to ensure it permits commercial use.

Focusing on completely legal sources not only protects you from infringement risks but can become a unique selling point for your business—you’re using ethically sourced materials. Your kids can watch you learn and adapt, showing them that perseverance and creativity matter more than cutting corners. You’ve got this.

2. Explore Creative Commons–Licensed Work  
   • On Flickr or Wikimedia, filter your search to “Creative Commons: Free to use” or similar. Pay attention to any attribution requirements, but you won’t have to deal with watermarks.  

3. Take Your Own Reference Photos  
   • Use your phone or camera to capture scenes around you—family, friends, pets, cityscapes. This gives you complete control over composition, lighting, and subject.

   • Offer something in return, like feedback or small sketches, to build goodwill and access more varied reference material.  

5. Study and Adapt Rather Than Trace  
   • Instead of tracing watermarked images, break down the shapes, proportions, and lighting you admire, then reconstruct them in your own way. This strengthens your skills and ensures your work remains original.  

6. Invest in Affordable Resources  
   • Look for budget-friendly art reference books or digital packs on sale.
